plan: Eight new SAT R&W items in the stricter hard-item design: convoluted (WIC), thinner bowls without the wheel (comparison-group inference), red autumn leaves alternative-function cross-text, diminishing-returns study table, egg-shape text structure, colon before an explanatory appositive, inverted-order agreement, in-other-words restatement. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: A late style
passages.text: The novelist's prose is usually praised as lucid, but in her final book the sentences grow deliberately ______, folding clause into clause until readers must go back to the beginning to follow them.

passages.title: Thinner bowls
passages.text: At an ancient village site, bowls made over a span of two centuries became steadily thinner-walled and more uniform in shape. Researchers had attributed the change to the arrival of the potter's wheel, which appears at the site at the start of that period. However, at a nearby village where potters never adopted the wheel, bowls from the same two centuries show the same gradual thinning. This suggests that ______

passages.title: Red autumn leaves
passages.text:
Text 1
Why do some trees turn red in autumn rather than simply yellow? One botanist argues that the red pigments act as a sunscreen: as a leaf withdraws its nutrients before falling, the pigments shield it from sunlight damage, allowing the tree to recover more of those nutrients.

Text 2
Ecologists comparing tree species across regions found that trees with red autumn leaves are especially common where leaf-eating insects that lay eggs in autumn are abundant. They propose that red coloring may advertise a tree's chemical defenses to these insects, discouraging them from laying eggs on it.

passages.title: Study time and scores
passages.text:
A school compared students' weekly study time with their average scores on a final exam.
0-2 hours per week: average score 62
3-5 hours per week: average score 74
6-8 hours per week: average score 79
9-11 hours per week: average score 81
A teacher concludes that students who studied more tended to score higher, but that each additional block of study time was associated with a smaller gain.

passages.title: Egg shapes
passages.text: Some birds lay eggs that are sharply pointed at one end. A long-standing explanation held that the shape keeps eggs from rolling off cliff ledges. Yet many pointed eggs are laid by birds that nest on flat ground. A study of eggs from more than 1,400 bird species found instead that egg shape is linked to flying ability: strong fliers tend to lay more elongated eggs, perhaps because a streamlined body limits how wide an egg can be.

passages.title: A traveling fungus
passages.text: After years of searching, the researchers finally identified the cause of the trees' ______ a fungus that had been carried into the region on imported timber.

passages.title: Willows on the bank
passages.text: Along the eroding riverbank, where volunteers planted cuttings last spring, ______ several species of willow that root easily and help hold the soil in place.

passages.title: Sunny-day flooding
passages.text: Many coastal cities now experience what planners call "sunny-day flooding." ______ streets near the shore fill with seawater during especially high tides, even when no rain has fallen.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: folding clause into clause until readers must go back to the beginning
candidates.explanation: Sentences that fold clause into clause and must be reread are intricate and hard to follow: "convoluted," in contrast to the usual lucidity.

A.rationale: Laconic writing uses very few words, the opposite of sentences that fold clause into clause.

B.rationale: Colloquial means informal or conversational; nothing suggests the sentences sound like everyday speech.

C.rationale: Effusive means gushing with feeling; the text describes complicated structure, not emotion.

hints: What does "folding clause into clause" describe?
candidates.remember: Use the contrast word and the description after the blank together.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the potter's wheel was adopted at both villages at the start of the same period.
choices.B: something besides the potter's wheel may have helped change the bowls at the first site.
choices.C: only the residents of the first village came to prefer thinner bowls.
choices.D: the potter's wheel caused bowls to become thicker and less uniform over time.

candidates.evidence: where potters never adopted the wheel, bowls from the same two centuries show the same gradual thinning
candidates.explanation: If bowls thinned in the same way where no wheel was used, the wheel cannot be the only explanation for the first site, so another factor may have contributed.

A.rationale: The text says potters at the nearby village never adopted the wheel.

C.rationale: The nearby village's bowls thinned too, so the preference was not limited to the first village.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests the wheel had this effect; the bowls at the wheel site became thinner.

hints: What does the nearby village show about the wheel's role?

strategy.explanation: Treat the second village as a comparison group.

candidates.remember: If an effect appears without the proposed cause, look for another cause.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the ecologists in Text 2 most likely respond to the botanist's argument in Text 1?

choices.A: They would suggest that red coloring may serve a function other than the one Text 1 proposes.
choices.B: They would argue that red pigments provide no protection at all from sunlight damage.
choices.C: They would agree that red leaves protect against sunlight, which explains the regional pattern they found.
choices.D: They would argue that trees with yellow leaves are better at recovering nutrients in autumn.

candidates.evidence: They propose that red coloring may advertise a tree's chemical defenses
candidates.explanation: Text 2 offers a different explanation (signaling to insects) without disproving Text 1's; the ecologists would suggest red may serve another purpose.

B.rationale: The ecologists propose another function; they do not test or deny protection from sunlight.

C.rationale: Their explanation of the regional pattern involves insects, not sunlight.

D.rationale: Neither text compares nutrient recovery in yellow and red trees.

hints: Does Text 2 disprove Text 1 or offer an alternative?

strategy.explanation: Check whether Text 2 tests Text 1's claim.

candidates.remember: An alternative explanation is not the same as a refutation.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the table to support the teacher's conclusion?

choices.A: Students who studied 9-11 hours per week averaged 81, the highest score of any group in the table.
choices.B: Each group that studied more averaged a higher score than the group that studied less than it did.
choices.C: Scores rose 12 points, then 5, then only 2 from each group to the next one up the table.
choices.D: Average scores rose a total of 19 points from the group studying least to the group studying most.

candidates.evidence: each additional block of study time was associated with a smaller gain
candidates.explanation: The gains between successive groups are 12, 5, and 2 points, so scores rise but each step adds less. Only C shows both parts.

A.rationale: This shows the top group scored highest but not that the gains shrank.

B.rationale: This supports only the first part of the conclusion, not the shrinking gains.

D.rationale: A total change hides whether the gains between groups grew or shrank.

hints: What would "a smaller gain" look like in the table?

strategy.explanation: Compute the differences between neighboring groups.

candidates.remember: Diminishing returns show up in the differences, not the totals.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It defends a traditional explanation of a trait against a challenge from newly gathered data.
choices.B: It compares the nesting habits of cliff-dwelling birds with those of ground-nesting birds in detail.
choices.C: It explains the methods researchers used to measure the eggs of more than 1,400 bird species.
choices.D: It introduces a trait, raises a problem for an old explanation, and reports evidence for another.

candidates.evidence: Yet many pointed eggs are laid by birds that nest on flat ground.
candidates.explanation: The text describes pointed eggs, shows a weakness in the cliff explanation (ground nesters), and then reports a study linking shape to flight.

A.rationale: The text does not defend the cliff explanation; it raises a problem with it.

B.rationale: Nesting sites are mentioned briefly as evidence, not compared in detail.

C.rationale: The text gives the study's finding, not its methods.

hints: What job does each sentence do?

strategy.explanation: Label the sentences in order, then match.

candidates.remember: Describe structure by the role of each part, in order.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: the researchers finally identified the cause of the trees'
candidates.explanation: The first part is a complete clause, and the noun phrase that follows names the cause. A colon can introduce such an explanation.

A.rationale: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "a fungus that had been carried ..." is a noun phrase.

C.rationale: This creates a comma splice: "it was a fungus ..." is an independent clause.

D.rationale: "Which a fungus that had been carried ..." is not a grammatical clause.

hints: Is the part after the blank a complete sentence?

strategy.explanation: Check what can follow a complete clause and introduce a noun phrase.

candidates.remember: A colon after a complete clause can introduce a noun phrase that explains it.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: In this inverted sentence the subject, "several species of willow," follows the verb. It is plural, so the verb is "grow."

A.rationale: The subject comes after the verb: "several species," which is plural.

B.rationale: "Is" is singular and does not agree with the plural "species."

D.rationale: "Has" is singular and does not agree with the plural "species."

hints: What is the subject of the verb?

strategy.explanation: Find the subject after the blank.

candidates.remember: In inverted sentences, look after the verb for the subject.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: even when no rain has fallen
candidates.explanation: The second sentence explains what "sunny-day flooding" means, restating the term in plain language, so "In other words" fits.

B.rationale: Nothing in the second sentence contrasts with the first.

C.rationale: The second sentence does not describe a separate, similar case; it explains the term.

D.rationale: The second sentence explains what the term means, not something caused by it.

hints: Does the second sentence define, contrast with, or result from the first?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: Use "in other words" when a sentence restates or explains a term.
